lesson.title: Dimensional Analysis: Turning Unit Conversions into an Automatic Skill
lesson.summary: Learn to chain conversion factors so units cancel like algebra, turning tricky unit-conversion and rate problems into simple, mechanical multiplication.
lesson.body:
Nearly every ACT unit-conversion or measurement question can be solved the same reliable way: by treating units as algebraic objects that multiply, divide, and cancel just like variables. This method, called dimensional analysis, replaces guesswork about whether to multiply or divide by a conversion number with a mechanical process: write each conversion fact as a fraction equal to one, then chain those fractions together so unwanted units cancel out, leaving only the units you want.

The key move is choosing which way to write each conversion fraction. Since 1 mile = 5,280 feet, that fact can be written as either 5,280 ft / 1 mi or 1 mi / 5,280 ft, both equal to 1, because the top and bottom describe the same distance. You pick whichever orientation cancels the unit you are trying to eliminate: if your starting quantity has miles on top, you want a conversion fraction with miles on the bottom, so the mile units cancel diagonally, leaving feet.

Worked example. A car travels at 45 miles per hour. Express this speed in feet per second. Start with the given rate and multiply by conversion fractions chosen so the units cancel: 45 mi/hr x (5,280 ft / 1 mi) x (1 hr / 3,600 s). The "mi" in the numerator of the first factor cancels with the "mi" in the denominator of the second factor, and the "hr" in the denominator of the first factor cancels with the "hr" in the numerator of the third factor, leaving only feet on top and seconds on the bottom. Now just multiply and divide the numbers: 45 x 5,280 = 237,600, and 237,600 / 3,600 = 66. So 45 miles per hour equals 66 feet per second.

A common trap on area and volume conversions is forgetting that the conversion factor must be squared or cubed along with the units. If 1 yard = 3 feet, then 1 square yard is not simply 3 square feet, it is 3 feet x 3 feet = 9 square feet, because both dimensions of the square are being converted. So to convert 3 square yards to square feet, multiply by 9, not 3: 3 yd² x 9 = 27 ft². The same idea applies in three dimensions: converting cubic yards to cubic feet requires multiplying by 3³ = 27, not by 3.

Finally, build the habit of sanity-checking your converted answer against a rough mental benchmark. A brisk human sprint is roughly 20 feet per second, and highway car speeds are much faster than a sprint, so an answer of 66 feet per second for a car going 45 mph feels reasonable, while an answer like 6.6 feet per second (a factor-of-ten slip) or 3,960 feet per second (forgetting to convert the hour to seconds) should immediately look wrong. The ACT's wrong-answer choices are frequently built from exactly these predictable slips, the right numbers but the wrong operation or a missing conversion step, so a quick magnitude check after you convert can catch an error before you bubble it in.
